# Wi-Fi Station Mode & Data Upload {.unnumbered}

Our ESP32 now wakes up from deep sleep on schedule. In this chapter, we add Wi-Fi.

Instead of just saving the data to the local SD card, the ESP32 will now connect to a local Wi-Fi network and upload the sensor readings to a server using an HTTP POST request.

## The Code

> **Ready-to-use project:** The complete code for this firmware is available in the repository here: [`06_wifi_station`](https://github.com/wg1d/personal-autonomous-weather-station/tree/main/firmware/PoC/Phase-03/06_wifi_station)

> **Further Reading:** For a deeper dive into Wi-Fi connectivity on the ESP32, you can refer to this excellent [uPesy tutorial on connecting an ESP32 to Wi-Fi](https://www.upesy.fr/blogs/tutorials/how-to-connect-wifi-acces-point-with-esp32).

### Code Cleanup Notice
As the firmware grows, the `setup()` function is getting long. In this chapter, the code keeps the structure of Phase 02: we insert the Wi-Fi logic right after the SD card write, so the chapter only shows this new part. In **Phase 04**, we will rebuild the firmware on a proper architecture.

### Connecting to a Network
To connect the ESP32 to the internet (or your local network), it needs to act as a **Wi-Fi Station**. Just like your smartphone or laptop, the ESP32 must know two pieces of information to connect to your router:

1. **SSID** (The name of the Wi-Fi network)
2. **Password**

### Securing Credentials with `secrets.h`
Hardcoding Wi-Fi passwords in the main code is a security risk as soon as you share the code or push it to GitHub.

To solve this, we create a template file called `secrets.example.h` inside our project folder:

```cpp
#ifndef SECRETS_H
#define SECRETS_H

// IMPORTANT: Do NOT commit your actual credentials to GitHub!
// 1. Copy this file to 'secrets.h' (which is ignored by Git)
// 2. Replace the placeholders below with your actual Wi-Fi credentials

const char* WIFI_SSID = "YOUR_WIFI_SSID";
const char* WIFI_PASSWORD = "YOUR_WIFI_PASSWORD";

#endif
```

We then add `secrets.h` to the project's `.gitignore` file. Anyone who clones the project copies the template to `secrets.h` and fills in their own credentials. The real passwords stay on your computer and are never committed.

### The Target Server
Before we can upload data, the ESP32 needs to know *where* to send it. At the top of your `.ino` file (right below the `WAKEUP_INTERVAL_SECONDS`), we define the IP address of our local computer which will soon host our dummy backend server:

```cpp
// Dummy server endpoint (Update with your computer's local IP address)
const char* serverName = "http://192.168.1.15:5000/upload";
```

> **Check your IP Address!** Make sure to replace `192.168.1.15` with your actual local network IP address, otherwise the ESP32 will fail to connect (Error `-1`).
> 
> **How to find your IP address:**
> - **Windows:** Open Command Prompt and type `ipconfig` (look for "IPv4 Address").
> - **macOS:** Open Terminal and type `ipconfig getifaddr en0`.
> - **Linux:** Open Terminal and type `hostname -I`.

### The Wi-Fi Upload Logic

In our main firmware, we `#include "secrets.h"` and add the upload logic right after saving to the SD card. 

Here is how the ESP32 handles the connection:

```cpp
  // 4. Upload Data via Wi-Fi
  WiFi.begin(WIFI_SSID, WIFI_PASSWORD);
  Serial.print("Connecting to WiFi...");
  
  // Timeout after 10 seconds to save battery if network is down
  int wifi_timeout = 0;
  while (WiFi.status() != WL_CONNECTED && wifi_timeout < 20) {
    delay(500);
    Serial.print(".");
    wifi_timeout++;
  }

  if(WiFi.status() == WL_CONNECTED) {
    Serial.println("\nConnected to WiFi network");
    HTTPClient http;
    http.begin(serverName); // Dummy server endpoint
    http.addHeader("Content-Type", "text/csv");
    
    // Open the CSV file from the SD card
    File file = SD.open("/weather_data.csv");
    if (file) {
      Serial.print("Uploading CSV file to server: ");
      Serial.println(serverName);
      
      // Stream the file directly to the server to save RAM
      int httpResponseCode = http.sendRequest("POST", &file, file.size());
      
      if (httpResponseCode > 0) {
        Serial.printf("HTTP Response code: %d\n", httpResponseCode);
      } else {
        Serial.printf("Error code: %d\n", httpResponseCode);
      }
      file.close();
    } else {
      Serial.println("Failed to open CSV file for uploading.");
    }
    http.end();
  } else {
    Serial.println("\nWiFi connection failed, skipped upload");
  }

  // Turn off Wi-Fi to save power before sleeping
  WiFi.disconnect(true);
  WiFi.mode(WIFI_OFF);
  
  // Power OFF the SD card module now that the upload is complete
  SD.end();
  digitalWrite(SD_OFF_PIN, LOW);
```

## How It Works

1.  **Timeouts Save Batteries:** Wi-Fi is by far the most power-hungry activity of the ESP32 (over 100 mA while connecting). If the router is offline, a plain `while(WiFi.status() != WL_CONNECTED)` loop would never exit, and the station would drain its battery within a day or two. We use a 10-second timeout: if the network isn't found, we skip the upload and go back to sleep.
2.  **Offline Tolerance (CSV Streaming):** Instead of uploading only the latest reading, we stream the *entire* `weather_data.csv` file from the SD card into the HTTP POST request. If the Wi-Fi goes down for 3 days, the ESP32 keeps saving data to the SD card; as soon as the Wi-Fi comes back, the next upload contains all the missed data, without any queuing logic.
    
> **Known Limitation:** The file grows forever, so each upload takes longer and costs more energy, and the server receives the same rows again and again. Connecting to Wi-Fi at every measurement is also expensive. With our [power budget](05-power-budget.qmd#cost-of-wi-fi) assumptions, one upload costs about $120\,mA \times 5\,s = 600\,mA \cdot s$. Spread over a 15-minute cycle, this adds $600\,mA \cdot s / 900\,s \approx 0.67\,mA$ to the average current, on top of the 0.18 mA of the station without Wi-Fi: about 5 times more in total. We accept these limitations to keep the PoC simple. The production architecture (Phase 4) uploads only the new rows, and less often.

3.  **Radio Shutdown:** Before sleeping, we call `WiFi.disconnect(true)` and `WiFi.mode(WIFI_OFF)`. Deep sleep powers the radio off anyway, but disconnecting cleanly tells the router that the station has left, and makes the intent explicit in the code.
4.  **Scheduling After a Long Wake-up:** With Wi-Fi, a wake-up can now last more than 10 seconds. As explained in Phase 02, the next alarm is computed from the time read *after* the upload, so it is never set in the past.

## Next Steps

The ESP32 now sends its data, but nothing is listening yet. In the next chapter, we build a dummy backend server to receive these POST requests.
